sections.report:
**Section.** The whole piece: applies. (Bash was refused, so I couldn't run `crop.mjs` or `entries.mjs`. The image is about one screen, 1280×800, so I worked from the whole image. Every checklist line came out yes, so no entries needed opening.)

**Findings**
None. Every line is yes.

These are copy points with no checklist line. They come from the "words are part of the design" rules in `agents/critic.md`, and the director can drop them if they belong to another section:
1. **Copy: the default card is never explained, and the opening paragraph seems to contradict "Remove an old card"** (no checklist line). The intro (y≈160–186) says "The new card is used from your next invoice," which reads as if an added card takes over billing by itself. "Remove an old card" (y≈475–501) then says a card can only be removed "once another card is set as the default," and no step on the page says how to set a default. A reader who adds a card and then tries to remove the old one may be blocked and won't know why. Is the new card the default automatically, or must they set it? Fix: say once, in "Add a new card," whether the new card becomes the default, and if it doesn't, give the step. This is a defect. Weight: major, because it is the main task on the page.
2. **Copy: "nothing already paid is moved" can be read two ways** (no checklist line). In the intro, line 2 (y≈186), "moved" could mean past payments aren't refunded to the old card, or that they aren't charged again to the new one. Money lines are what readers hold the company to. Fix: say it plainly, e.g. "Payments you've already made stay on your old card." This is a defect. Weight: minor.
3. **Copy: "After a third failed try" is clipped** (no checklist line). It sits in "If a payment fails" (y≈600–627). The reader has to work out that "try" means a payment attempt, and it is unclear whether the email also goes out after the third failure. Fix: "If the third attempt also fails, your account becomes read-only until a payment goes through." This is taste. Weight: minor.

**What's working.**
- It reads as one plain thing. The breadcrumb, H1, three task headings and short paragraphs make a help-centre article clear within a second, and it has no ornament to filter out. One quiet grey-and-black typeface fits a calm, practical billing page.
- The H2s are the tasks themselves ("Add a new card," "Remove an old card," "If a payment fails"), so a reader can scan straight to their situation.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 8 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

sections.report:
**Walk (working notes).** Image is about one screen (1280×800), so I worked from the whole image. The crop script was not run because Bash is denied.

First read: the eye lands on "Changing your payment card" (bold, about 36 px, y≈108). It then drops to the intro and steps down through three bold subheads: "Add a new card", "Remove an old card" and "If a payment fails". This reads as a help-centre article for a customer changing billing details. It feels calm, plain and orderly. Assumed job: let a customer find the right task quickly and follow it.

What matters first:
- One element dominates? **yes.** The title is roughly twice the body size, in heavy weight and near-black. Nothing competes with it.
- Levels distinct, no near-equal sizes? **yes.** I count four levels:
  - breadcrumb: about 17 px, grey, regular
  - title: about 36 px, bold
  - subheads: about 21 px, bold
  - body: about 17 px, regular

  The breadcrumb and body share a size but are told apart by colour and position. Subhead and body differ in size and weight.
- Headings differ by more than size? **yes.** The subheads are bold against regular body text.

No `no` or `unsure` lines, so there are no entries to open.

---

**Section.** What matters first: applies.

**Findings**
None.

(This is outside my section, for the arrangement critic. Each subhead sits about as far from the text above it as from the text below. For example, "Add a new card" has a gap of about 38 px above it, from the intro ending at y≈186, and about 37 px below it to the body at y≈285. So each subhead floats between sections instead of sitting with its own section.)

**What's working.**
- **One clear entry point.** The title is about 36 px bold, near-black, at y≈108. It is the only large element on the page, and it says exactly what the article covers. A customer knows they're in the right place within a second.
- **A short, clean type scale.** There are four levels with big steps between them. The subheads use both size and weight to separate them from the body (Refactoring UI: bolder, not bigger), and the breadcrumb is set back by grey rather than by another size. The three task subheads can be scanned straight down the left edge, which fits a reader looking for one task.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 3 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Is the space inside each group clearly smaller than the space between groups, so each heading sits nearer the text it introduces?** Each H2 sits about the same distance from the paragraph above it as from the text it introduces. Gaps by eye, with no measured facts file:

   | Heading | Gap above | Gap below |
   |---|---|---|
   | "Add a new card" | ~32 px (y≈193→225) | ~30 px (y≈247→277) |
   | "Remove an old card" | ~30 px (y≈385→415) | ~28 px (y≈437→465) |
   | "If a payment fails" | ~30 px (y≈510→540) | ~29 px (y≈562→591) |

   - **What the viewer experiences:** the headings float halfway between sections. Section breaks show only through bold weight, not space, so the page reads as an even stack of lines rather than three separate tasks. A customer scanning for "remove a card" gets less help finding where each task begins and ends.
   - **Why:** proximity grouping. Equal gaps erase the groups, and a label should sit nearer its own content than the one before it (Arnheim, *Art and Visual Perception*, ch. II, on Wertheimer's rule of proximity).
   - **Fix:** about double the space above each H2 and cut the space below it to about a third of that, so each heading clearly belongs to its paragraph. The two paragraphs under "Add a new card" can keep their ~20 px gap, which already reads as one group.
   - **Type and weight:** defect, minor. The bold headings still carry the structure, and the article is short.

2. **Does the visual weight balance, with no side, crowded or empty, that makes the page look about to tip?** All content sits in a column from x≈160 to x≈840. The left margin is 160 px, while about 440 px on the right (x≈840–1280) is empty for the full height.
   - **What the viewer experiences:** the column looks pushed left. The empty right side looks like a sidebar ("In this article", contact support, related articles) that is missing or failed to load, not like space that was chosen.
   - **Why:** a heavy side needs a counterweight (Arnheim, *Art and Visual Perception*, ch. I "Balance"). Left-aligned reading columns are normal, so this is a judgment call, not a broken rule.
   - **Fix:** if the template has a right rail, it should appear here. If it doesn't, centre the column or widen the left margin, so the empty space reads as margin rather than as a hole.
   - **Type and weight:** taste, minor.

**What's working.**
- **One shared left edge:** everything shares the x≈160 edge, from the breadcrumb and H1 to the subheads and body. There are no near-misses, so the page reads as one ordered column, and the eye moves straight down without detours.
- **Even spacing in the header:** breadcrumb → H1 → intro have tight, even gaps (~20–25 px), so the header reads as one unit before the sections begin.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** Whether the empty right side is the intended layout, or a sidebar or nav that didn't render at this width. Check it in a live browser at 1280 px.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 11 yes, 2 no (space inside groups smaller than between groups; visual weight balances)

sections.report:
**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Do paragraph lines run about 45 to 75 characters?** No. The text column runs from x≈160 to x≈840, and the lines look to be about 77 to 85 characters long. "A card can be removed once another card is set as the default. Select the card, then" (y≈474) is about 84, and the intro's first line (y≈160) is about 77. The paragraphs are only two lines each, so the extra width costs little here: the eye returns to the left edge only once or twice per paragraph. Bringhurst gives 45 to 75 characters, about 66 ideal (*Elements of Typographic Style* 2.1.2). Fix: narrow the column to about 600–620 px at this size, which also keeps the article clear of the empty right half. Convention. Weight: minor.
2. **Do paragraphs and columns break cleanly, with no lone short word on a last line?** No. "days." sits alone on the last line of the hold paragraph (x≈160, y≈376). That leaves a one-word line with a gap above it, right under the "Add a new card" steps, and it makes the paragraph look like it ends twice. Source: Bringhurst 2.4.2. Fix: narrow the measure (finding 1 will likely reflow it) or allow a balanced/pretty text-wrap on body paragraphs. Convention. Weight: minor.

Copy, which no checklist line covers but which the director should weigh:
3. **The failed-payment rule can be read two ways** (y≈600–627). "We try again after three days and email the account owner each time" could mean one retry three days later, or a retry every three days. "After a third failed try the account moves to read-only" has no comma after "try", so it reads as "a third failed try the account" until the reader backs up. This is the only deadline on the page that the reader acts on: misreading it means not knowing how long they have before the account locks. Fix: say it as a sequence with the timing spelled out, e.g. "If a payment fails, we try again every three days and email the account owner each time. If the third try fails, your account becomes read-only until a payment goes through." Defect. Weight: major for the page's job, small for type.

**What's working.**
- One sans family carries everything in three clear steps: H1 ~36px bold, H2 ~20px bold, body ~17px regular, plus a grey breadcrumb. Every size has an obvious job, with no near-miss sizes, and weight does the finer work.
- The body has comfortable leading (about 1.5) and is set flush left with a gentle rag. Short chunked paragraphs under task-named headings ("Add a new card", "Remove an old card", "If a payment fails") are exactly what someone scanning a help page needs.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 28 yes, 2 no (lines of 45 to 75 characters; widows, orphans, and runts), 0 unsure

Walk (working notes). First read: the eye lands on the bold H1 "Changing your payment card", then moves down the bold H2s. It reads as a plain help-centre article with a calm, neutral feel and no colour at all. Assumed job: a help article that helps a customer change or remove a card and understand what happens when a payment fails.

Color section:
- Small palette: yes (near-black text, slate-gray breadcrumb, white).
- Saturated color kept to a small share: yes (there is none).
- Clear range of light and dark: yes (the dark headings and body text on white carry all the structure).
- Warm forward, cool back: yes (no temperature at play; the cool gray breadcrumb sits back, which is right).
- Matching colors look the same: yes.
- No vibrating edges: yes.
- Status colors used for their usual meaning: yes (none used).
- Meaning not shown by color alone: yes. The breadcrumb is set apart by gray, but also by its position and the › separator. Whether its parts look like links is a question for the interface section.
- Dark theme background: yes (light theme, so this doesn't apply).

No line answered no or unsure, so I didn't open any entries.

**Section.** Color: applies. The page is almost entirely neutral, and every line passes.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- Light and dark do all the work. The near-black headings and body text sit on white at what looks like full contrast, so the page's structure holds in grayscale with nothing to lose. For a help page that people scan for one answer, that's the right call.
- The breadcrumb ("Help centre › Billing", about x 160–317, y 50–70) is the only element with a different colour, a muted slate gray. That pushes the way-finding text back behind the H1 without a smaller size or a second hue, which is the "lighter, not smaller" move (Refactoring UI).

sections.report:
**Section.** Interface: applies. The only controls are the two breadcrumb links, "Help centre" and "Billing".

**Findings**
1. **Does the screen put what the user likely needs next in front of them** and **Is everything the user needs to act visible on this screen, with nothing to remember from another?** Both lines are about one problem. The page is about changing a card, but it never links to the place where you do it.
   - **Where:** The "Add a new card" step (x 160–811, y 275–322) spells out a path, "Open Settings, choose Billing, and select Add card". "Remove an old card" (y 465–512) and "If a payment fails" (y 590–637) also describe actions with no way to take them.
   - **What the viewer meets:** They have to memorise the three-step path, leave the help centre, and find Settings on their own. The reader of "If a payment fails" is the one most likely to be stressed and short of time, and they get no route to fix the card that failed.
   - **Why:** Nielsen 6, Recognition rather than recall: the user should not have to carry information from one screen to another. The anticipation point has no approved source, so that part is common sense.
   - **Fix:** Turn the path into a direct link, or add a button such as "Go to Billing settings" or "Add a card" under the "Add a new card" heading. Repeat the link in the payment-failure section. Keep the written path for people who aren't signed in.
   - **Type and weight:** Defect, major.
2. **Does every control look like what it does, … links marked by more than color?** The breadcrumb doesn't look like links.
   - **Where:** "Help centre › Billing", top left (x 160–317, y 50–72).
   - **What the viewer meets:** It's set as grey regular text with no underline, so it reads as a label. A reader who wants other billing articles or the help centre home may not see that it's their way back up.
   - **Why:** "Buttons and links must look clickable" (WCAG 1.4.1 Use of Color; NN/g, Moran 2017, partly confirmed). The grey is also the same muted colour you would use for metadata, which makes the label reading stronger.
   - **Fix:** Use a link colour with an underline, or at least underline on hover and focus. Keep the current page out of the trail, as it is now.
   - **Type and weight:** Convention, minor.
3. **Are shortcuts offered for frequent actions, such as search, filters, or keyboard hints?** The page has no search and no "contact support" route.
   - **Where:** Nowhere on the screen. The breadcrumb is the only control.
   - **What the viewer meets:** If the article doesn't answer their question (for example, why removing a card fails), the only move left is going back up the breadcrumb and browsing.
   - **Why:** Nielsen 7, Flexibility and efficiency of use. A help centre without search also breaks what users expect from help centres (Jakob's law).
   - **Fix:** Add a help-centre search field above the breadcrumb, and a "Still stuck? Contact support" line at the end of the article.
   - **Type and weight:** Convention, minor. If the site header was cropped out of this capture, see below.

**What's working.**
- The instructions name the controls by their visible labels ("Add card", "Remove", "confirm"), not by position or colour. A reader can match each word to the button they'll see.
- The breadcrumb shows where the reader is ("Billing") and leaves the current page out of the trail. That follows the usual pattern and gives a clear way back up.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- Whether the breadcrumb links show a visible focus indicator, and an underline on hover or focus.
- Whether a site header with search and navigation sits above this view and was cropped out of the capture. If it exists, finding 3 mostly goes away. Check in a live browser.

**Checklist.** Interface: 33 lines, 28 yes, 4 no (controls look like what they do; recognition rather than recall; shortcuts such as search; puts what the user needs next in front of them), 1 unsure (focus indicator)
